title: Chayei Sarah: two sons at the grave (Genesis 25:9)
hook: Isaac and Ishmael, long apart, bury their father together

segments.voice: Yesterday, Mincha: Isaac in the field at evening, and the afternoon prayer. Your line was the field at evening.

Two siblings who haven't spoken in years, standing at the same graveside. It happens at funerals sometimes. Maybe they don't hug. Maybe they barely look at each other. But they're both there, both holding a shovel. Genesis tells a story like that. Abraham had two sons: Ishmael, the older, whose mother Hagar was sent away when he was a boy, and Isaac, the younger, Sarah's son. The two grew up apart. Years pass. Then their father dies.
screen: `SIBLINGS AT A GRAVESIDE.` → `ISHMAEL, SENT AWAY.` → `ISAAC, WHO STAYED.`

segments.voice: The Torah gives Abraham a gentle ending. He dies in a good old age, an old man and satisfied with his years, and is gathered to his people. A hundred and seventy-five years. Then one short, quiet verse: Isaac and Ishmael his sons buried him in the cave of Machpelah, next to Sarah, in the field Abraham bought at full price. That's all. No speech, no reconciliation scene. Just two names, side by side, doing the last thing a son can do. The text doesn't tell us whether they talked. The rabbis noticed the order of the names. Ishmael is older, yet Isaac is named first. Rashi, following the Talmud, reads that as a sign that Ishmael had made teshuvah, that he'd turned, and let his younger brother go ahead of him. There are hints earlier, too. Just before meeting Rebekah, Isaac is coming from a place called Beer-lahai-roi, the well where an angel found Hagar in the desert, years before. A midrash, which Rashi repeats, says Isaac had gone there to bring Hagar back to his father. The text only tells us where he was coming from. After the funeral, the Torah stays with Ishmael for a moment. It lists his twelve sons, princes of their tribes, just as God had promised Abraham, and tells us Ishmael lived a hundred and thirty-seven years. He isn't written out of the story. Families break, and the text doesn't pretend this one fully healed. But it gives the two brothers, side by side at their father's grave, a verse of their own.
screen: `ABRAHAM, OLD AND SATISFIED.` · `ISAAC AND ISHMAEL BURIED HIM.` · `THE YOUNGER NAMED FIRST.` · `ISHMAEL'S TWELVE PRINCES.` · then, large: `BROTHERS AT THE GRAVE.`

segments.voice: Think of someone you've drifted from, a sibling, a cousin, an old friend, and whether anything hard is happening for them right now: an illness, a loss, a move. Picture being in the same room with them, not fixing the past, just being there. Let one small way of showing up come to mind: a text, a card, a call.
Chayei Sarah. The life of Sarah, a portion that ends with Abraham's burial, and his two sons, long apart, together at the grave.
Your line: brothers at the grave. Side by side, even unhealed. Day one hundred eighty-five, done.

howItsDone: At a Jewish funeral, family and friends often take turns placing earth on the coffin with a shovel, and the mourners then sit shivah together in the week that follows.
